artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let $D(P)$ denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points in $P$. A planar $n$-point set $P$ is called near-optimal if $D(P)=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ (this matches, up to constants, the lower bound of Guth–Katz and the upper bound achieved by the $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ integer grid).

A constant-degree algebraic curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the zero set of a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbb{R}[x,y]$ whose degree is bounded by an absolute constant.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $C=C(\varepsilon)$ such that for every near-optimal planar $n$-point set $P$ and every constant-degree algebraic curve $\gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, the number of points of $P$ lying on $\gamma$ is at most $C\,n^{1/2+\varepsilon}$.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. Surveys and recent papers on distinct distances continue to cite the best known bound on the number of points of a near-optimal set on a constant-degree algebraic curve as O(n^{43/52}) (improving O(n^{7/8})), still far from the conjectured O(n^{1/2+ε}). No resolution of the conjecture was found in the search results.
